title: The Power of Communication
goals: I can summarize the reading’s main point in my own words.
I can point to two details that support my summary.
I can identify a problem and its solution in a short spoken account.
I can check a detail by asking for clarification.
I can give an opinion with two reasons and an example.
I can ask a follow-up question that responds to my partner’s idea.
I can organize a presentation into an opening, three points, and a conclusion.
I can make important words stand out without stressing every word.
dialogue: Mina: I think good listeners should ask more questions.
Omar: What kind of questions do you mean?
Mina: Questions that check meaning. Yesterday I misunderstood where our group was meeting.
Omar: So a question could clear up a misunderstanding?
Mina: Exactly. We also need to take turns, rather than interrupt.
Omar: I agree. Could asking too many questions interrupt the speaker as well?
notice: Omar does more than agree: he checks Mina’s meaning and then asks about a possible limit to her idea.
response: For me, listening is the most important communication skill. First, taking turns gives everyone a chance to make their point. Second, careful listening helps us clear up a misunderstanding before it becomes an argument. Last week, a classmate thought I had rejected his idea. I asked him to explain, then repeated what I had understood. We realized we were talking about different parts of the task. That taught me not to jump to conclusions. Listening also helps me support my opinion: I can answer the point someone actually made, rather than the point I expected to hear.
frames: My main point is…
One reason is… A second reason is…
Could you explain what you mean by…?
transfer: Discuss the most useful skill for a new club member. Give your own example and ask your partner one question about theirs.

listening.title: The meeting that almost went wrong
listening.script: Our study club usually meets in Room Two at four in the afternoon. Last Monday, the organizer sent a short message: Meet in the new room at the usual time. I knew the time, but I did not know which room was new. Instead of guessing, I asked for the room number. The organizer replied that we should use Room Five because Room Two needed repairs. I repeated the plan back: Room Five, four o’clock, Monday. She confirmed it and sent a clearer message to the whole group. Before the meeting, I also asked who was bringing the books. It turned out that nobody had agreed to bring them, so I offered. We started on time, and everyone had something to read.

questions.prompt: What caused the uncertainty?
questions.answer: The message said new room without giving a room number.
questions.evidence: I did not know which room was new.

questions.prompt: Which room did the club use?
questions.evidence: we should use Room Five

questions.prompt: Why was the usual room unavailable?
questions.evidence: Room Two needed repairs

questions.prompt: How did the speaker check the meeting plan?
questions.answer: By repeating the room, time, and day back and receiving confirmation.
questions.evidence: I repeated the plan back: Room Five, four o’clock, Monday.

questions.prompt: What responsibility did the speaker take on?
questions.evidence: nobody had agreed to bring them, so I offered

listening.gist: A club member clarifies an unclear plan and helps the meeting run smoothly.

title: The Art of Goal Setting
goals: I can explain the difference between a wish and an action plan.
I can support my explanation with an example from the reading.
I can identify a goal, an obstacle, and a revised plan in a spoken account.
I can distinguish what was planned from what actually happened.
I can explain a realistic goal and ask about a partner’s constraints.
I can negotiate a smaller next step when a plan is difficult.
I can present a goal with actions and a way to check progress.
I can pause between ideas so listeners can follow my plan.
dialogue: Farid: I want to become a confident speaker this month.
Leila: What would that look like in practice?
Farid: I’d like to explain an idea for two minutes without reading a script.
Leila: How much time can you set aside?
Farid: Ten minutes on three evenings. I can record a short attempt, or just practise aloud.
Leila: That sounds manageable. How will you check whether your message is clearer?
notice: Leila asks what the goal means and what time is available before suggesting a solution.
response: My goal is to explain an idea for two minutes using only keyword notes. I can set aside ten minutes on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday. First, I’ll choose a familiar topic and make a short plan. Then I’ll speak, note where I got stuck, and try again. After two weeks, I’ll ask a willing partner to summarize my main point. If they cannot follow it, I’ll work on my organization rather than simply trying to speak faster. When an evening is busy, my fallback is a one-minute attempt, not giving up for the whole week.
frames: By…, I want to be able to…
The main obstacle might be…
If that happens, my next step will be…
transfer: Plan a small learning goal for a fictional student who has limited time. Explain how you would tell whether the plan is working.

listening.title: A smaller plan that lasted
listening.script: At the beginning of the month, I planned to learn twenty new English words every evening. On the first day I did it, but by Thursday I was tired and had stopped. My friend asked what I actually wanted to do with the words. I said I wanted to take part in class discussions. We made a smaller plan: on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, I would choose two useful expressions and use them in a short spoken response. Each practice would take ten minutes. After two weeks, I would check whether I could explain a point without writing every sentence first. I missed one evening, but I returned to the plan on Friday. I had learned fewer new words than I originally intended, yet I was practising the skill I wanted to improve.

questions.prompt: What was the original daily target?
questions.answer: Twenty new English words every evening.
questions.evidence: twenty new English words every evening

questions.prompt: What did the speaker actually want to do?
questions.evidence: I wanted to take part in class discussions

questions.prompt: On which three days would the new practice happen?
questions.evidence: on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday

questions.prompt: How long would each practice take?
questions.evidence: Each practice would take ten minutes.

questions.prompt: When would the speaker review the plan?
questions.evidence: After two weeks, I would check

listening.gist: A learner replaces an ambitious word target with a smaller plan connected to speaking.

title: Emotional Intelligence
goals: I can explain an emotional skill using an everyday example.
I can distinguish what the reading says from my own interpretation.
I can identify a speaker’s first assumption and the information that changes it.
I can support my interpretation with a detail I heard.
I can acknowledge a concern and check that I understood it.
I can suggest a respectful response without diagnosing another person’s feelings.
I can organize a presentation about a communication strategy.
I can use pace and intonation to make my intention easier to understand.
dialogue: Nadia: My partner changed our slides without asking me. I felt ignored.
Samir: Was the main problem the changes, or not being asked?
Nadia: Not being asked. Some of the changes were helpful.
Samir: Have you told your partner that?
Nadia: Not yet. I could say I appreciate the work, but I want us to discuss changes first.
Samir: That explains your concern without assuming why your partner did it.
notice: Samir checks which part of the situation matters instead of immediately taking sides.
response: I think pausing before responding can help when a conversation becomes tense. It gives me time to separate what happened from what I assume it means. If a classmate changes my work, I might assume they do not respect me. But they may think they are helping. I would explain the effect on me and ask what they intended. That does not mean I must accept every change. It means I can discuss a boundary without beginning with an accusation. I can then suggest that we agree on changes together next time.
frames: It sounds as though your concern is…
Have I understood that correctly?
What would make the next step fair to both people?
transfer: Use a fictional group-project disagreement. Explain two possible interpretations before proposing a response. Do not disclose private conflict.

listening.title: Before making an assumption
listening.script: During our group project, Kareem spoke very little. At first, I thought he was not interested. I nearly told the teacher that he was not helping. Instead, I asked him privately whether the task was clear. He said he understood it, but the group moved so quickly that he could not find a moment to speak. He had already written several useful suggestions in his notebook. At the next meeting, we gave everyone a minute to explain one idea without interruption. Kareem suggested a simpler way to organize our presentation, and we used it. I learned that silence did not tell me enough about his effort or interest. Asking a question gave me information that my first assumption had missed.

questions.prompt: What did the speaker first assume about Kareem?
questions.evidence: I thought he was not interested

questions.prompt: Did Kareem understand the task?
questions.evidence: He said he understood it

questions.prompt: What made it difficult for him to contribute?
questions.answer: The group moved too quickly for him to find a turn.
questions.evidence: the group moved so quickly that he could not find a moment to speak

questions.prompt: What change did the group make?
questions.answer: Everyone received a minute to explain an idea without interruption.
questions.evidence: we gave everyone a minute to explain one idea without interruption

questions.prompt: What did Kareem contribute?
questions.answer: A simpler way to organize the presentation.
questions.evidence: a simpler way to organize our presentation

listening.gist: A question reveals why a quiet group member has not been speaking.

title: Money and Happiness
goals: I can summarize two ways money may affect people’s choices.
I can explain a trade-off without assuming everyone has the same priorities.
I can identify a spoken budget decision and the reasons for it.
I can check the numbers I hear.
I can compare spending options and negotiate a shared decision.
I can explain one benefit and one cost of our choice.
I can present a balanced position on money and well-being.
I can identify which claims need evidence and which are personal opinions.
dialogue: Amina: I’d spend the club’s money on a social event.
Bilal: I can see the benefit. My priority would be better lighting.
Amina: Why lighting rather than an event?
Bilal: People use the room every week, and some cannot read comfortably there.
Amina: Could we improve the room now and plan a free event?
Bilal: That might work. We should still ask the other members what they need.
notice: The speakers discuss the effect of each choice and look for a compromise rather than judging each other’s priorities.
response: If our learning club had a small budget, I would first ask what stops members from taking part. A celebration might be enjoyable, but better lighting could help people use the room every week. I would compare those benefits before deciding. The drawback is that practical improvements may not meet the need for friendship and relaxation. We could improve the room and arrange a free activity together. That is not the right choice for every club; it depends on what members need. My main point is that the price of an activity does not tell us its value.
frames: Our priority could be… because…
The benefit is…, but the trade-off is…
Could we agree on…?
transfer: Allocate 100 imaginary credits among two or three options you invent. Check the total and explain a rejected option. Personal income is not part of the task.

listening.title: One hundred credits
listening.script: Our learning club had one hundred imaginary credits for a planning exercise. We could buy books for forty credits, improve the lighting for thirty-five, or hold an event for thirty. Buying all three would cost more than we had. Some members wanted the event because new students had not met one another. Others said the room was too dark for reading. We agreed to buy the books and improve the lighting, leaving twenty-five credits unspent. For the new students, we planned a free conversation afternoon instead of the paid event. Not everyone preferred that choice, but each person had a chance to explain their reasons. Before ending the meeting, we wrote down the total and agreed to ask members whether the changes helped them use the room.

questions.prompt: How many credits did the club have?
questions.evidence: one hundred imaginary credits

questions.prompt: What did the books cost?
questions.evidence: buy books for forty credits

questions.prompt: Which two paid options did the club choose?
questions.evidence: buy the books and improve the lighting

questions.prompt: How many credits remained?
questions.evidence: leaving twenty-five credits unspent

questions.prompt: What replaced the paid event?
questions.evidence: a free conversation afternoon instead of the paid event

listening.gist: Club members explain different priorities and agree on a budget compromise.

title: Living with AI
goals: I can explain a possible AI use and a limitation.
I can distinguish a possibility from a claim supported by evidence.
I can identify an error and the steps used to check it.
I can explain which details in the account were verified.
I can propose a responsible classroom AI rule and consider an exception.
I can respond to a counterargument without dismissing it.
I can present an AI-related proposal with a drawback and checking process.
I can identify my sources and say when I am uncertain.
dialogue: Zara: I used a tool to suggest an outline, but one of its examples looks wrong.
Hadi: What makes you doubt it?
Zara: It gives a precise number without saying where it came from.
Hadi: Could you find the original source?
Zara: Not yet. I’ll leave the number out and use an example I can explain.
Hadi: You can also say how the tool helped, so the class knows which work is yours.
notice: The speakers describe the specific evidence problem; they do not assume that confidence or precision makes an answer reliable.
response: I would allow AI tools for brainstorming, but not as a substitute for checking facts or doing our own speaking. A suggested outline can help me get started. The risk is that I might repeat a convincing claim without understanding it. My rule would be to check factual claims against identifiable sources and explain what assistance I used. I would not upload classmates’ private information. If a tool is unavailable, the task should still be possible with paper and a partner. That keeps access fair and makes the speaking practice, rather than the technology, the main purpose.
frames: The tool may help with…, provided that…
The claim needs checking because…
I cannot verify that yet, so…
transfer: Write two proposed AI-use rules for a fictional speaking class. Explain how each protects learning or privacy. No AI account is needed.

listening.title: A confident answer was not enough
listening.script: I asked an AI tool to help me draft an announcement for our club meeting. It produced a clear paragraph and said we would meet on Thursday in Room Three. I had not given it those details. Before sharing the announcement, I checked the noticeboard. The actual meeting was on Wednesday in Room Five. I corrected the day and room, then asked the organizer to check the whole message. I kept the tool’s suggested order of information because it was useful, but I did not trust the invented details. I also left classmates’ phone numbers out of the tool. When I shared the final announcement, I explained that a tool had helped with the draft and that the organizer had confirmed the meeting information.

questions.prompt: Which day did the tool invent?
questions.evidence: meet on Thursday in Room Three

questions.prompt: What were the verified day and room?
questions.evidence: on Wednesday in Room Five

questions.prompt: Where did the speaker first check the meeting details?
questions.evidence: I checked the noticeboard

questions.prompt: What part of the draft did the speaker keep?
questions.evidence: I kept the tool’s suggested order of information

questions.prompt: What private information was kept out of the tool?
questions.evidence: I also left classmates’ phone numbers out of the tool.

listening.gist: A learner keeps useful drafting help but verifies invented details before sharing a message.

title: Is Love Enough?
goals: I can explain why a long-term partnership may need more than goodwill.
I can use a fictional relationship or a neutral team example without personal disclosure.
I can identify differing expectations and an agreed next step in a spoken account.
I can distinguish agreement from an unresolved question.
I can discuss expectations respectfully and acknowledge another viewpoint.
I can negotiate a concrete responsibility without judging another person’s beliefs.
I can present a balanced answer with reasons and an example.
I can use regular past-tense endings intelligibly when describing an experience.
dialogue: Lina: Do you think liking someone is enough to make a partnership work?
Yusuf: It helps, but shared expectations matter too. Think about running a club together.
Lina: One person might expect a meeting every week and the other once a month.
Yusuf: Exactly. Neither plan is automatically wrong, but the difference needs discussing.
Lina: So goodwill does not replace an agreement about responsibilities.
Yusuf: I agree, though an agreement also needs reviewing when circumstances change.
notice: The speakers use a neutral club example to discuss a broader partnership question. Learners may choose this route instead of personal relationship discussion.
response: Goodwill matters in a partnership, but I do not think it is enough on its own. People can care about one another and still expect different things. In a fictional reading club, one organizer might expect weekly meetings while the other can help only once a month. Without discussing that difference, each could feel let down. I would suggest agreeing on responsibilities and reviewing the plan after a few meetings. An agreement cannot prevent every problem, but it gives people something clear to discuss. For me, respect includes being honest about what we can and cannot promise.
frames: One expectation worth discussing is…
I understand that view; my concern is…
A fair agreement could include…
transfer: Choose a fictional club, project partnership, or adult relationship. Explain one shared expectation and one point that needs negotiation. Assessment concerns communication, not your beliefs.

listening.title: Friends with different plans
listening.script: Two friends, Mariam and Salim, offered to run a community reading club. They both liked the idea, but they had not discussed the work involved. Mariam expected to meet every week. Salim could help only once a month because of his work schedule. Their first conversation became tense because each thought the other had changed the plan. When they compared their notes, they realized they had never agreed on a schedule. They decided to hold one meeting a month for the first three months. Mariam would choose a short reading, and Salim would arrange the room. They would share the task of welcoming new members. They still needed to decide how to pay for printing, so they wrote that question down for their next conversation.

questions.prompt: How often did Mariam first expect to meet?
questions.evidence: Mariam expected to meet every week.

questions.prompt: Why could Salim help only monthly?
questions.evidence: because of his work schedule

questions.prompt: What schedule did they agree to try?
questions.answer: One meeting a month for the first three months.
questions.evidence: one meeting a month for the first three months

questions.prompt: Who would arrange the room?
questions.evidence: Salim would arrange the room

questions.prompt: Which question remained unresolved?
questions.evidence: They still needed to decide how to pay for printing

listening.gist: Two friends discover an unstated difference in expectations and agree on a trial plan.

title: Globalization
goals: I can explain a local–global connection using a concrete example.
I can describe a possible benefit and a possible cost.
I can identify a proposal, a concern, and a trial arrangement in a spoken account.
I can separate a prediction from a reported result.
I can compare how a proposal may affect different groups.
I can help a group reach a decision while acknowledging uncertainty.
I can present a recommendation with evidence and a limitation.
I can make key topic words clear enough for listeners to follow my argument.
dialogue: Roya: An online market could help our craft sellers reach more customers.
Aziz: It could, but what about shipping costs?
Roya: That is a real concern. We could start with local collection.
Aziz: Then how would sellers without internet take part?
Roya: Perhaps the community center could help them list their work, with permission.
Aziz: I’d support a small trial if we check both the costs and who is being left out.
notice: Each proposed benefit is tested against an access or cost question. The speakers do not treat a prediction as an established result.
response: I would support a small trial of an online craft market rather than assuming it will benefit everyone. It might help sellers find customers, but shipping costs and internet access could limit participation. A local collection option would reduce one problem. A shared support session could help with another, provided sellers control what is posted. After a month, we could compare costs, orders, and participants’ feedback. We would also ask who could not take part. The trial might show that the idea needs changing. That would be useful evidence, not a reason to hide the difficulties.
frames: This may benefit…, while…
A possible cost or barrier is…
Before extending the trial, we should check…
transfer: Propose a small local–global project. Consider two groups affected by it and identify one result that would change your recommendation.

listening.title: Testing an online market
listening.script: A community center invited six craft sellers to try an online market. Some sellers hoped to reach customers in other countries, but the organizers were worried about shipping costs. They decided to begin with local collection for one month. Sellers without reliable internet could bring product descriptions to the center, where a volunteer would help prepare listings with their permission. The group agreed to record the number of orders, the costs, and the time each seller spent on the trial. They also planned to ask people who could not take part what had stopped them. No one knew yet whether the market would be worth continuing. At the end of the month, they would review the information together before deciding whether to expand.

questions.prompt: How many sellers were invited?
questions.evidence: invited six craft sellers

questions.prompt: What cost worried the organizers?
questions.evidence: worried about shipping costs

questions.prompt: How long would the local collection trial last?
questions.evidence: local collection for one month

questions.prompt: How could sellers without reliable internet get help?
questions.answer: Bring descriptions to the center for a volunteer to help prepare listings, with permission.
questions.evidence: a volunteer would help prepare listings with their permission

questions.prompt: Had they already decided to expand the market?
questions.answer: No; they would review the information before deciding.
questions.evidence: review the information together before deciding whether to expand

listening.gist: A community plans a limited market trial and decides what evidence to collect before expanding.

title: Lingua Franca
goals: I can explain why people use a shared language across language backgrounds.
I can discuss a benefit and a challenge without ranking accents as superior.
I can identify an expression that causes confusion and its clarification.
I can explain the practical instructions I heard.
I can replace an unclear expression with plain language.
I can check understanding without making a listener feel embarrassed.
I can adapt a short presentation for a multilingual audience.
I can use clear pacing, phrasing, and repair when a listener needs help.
dialogue: Tariq: At the start, we’ll break the ice.
Elena: Could you explain that expression?
Tariq: Of course. We’ll do a short activity to help people feel comfortable talking.
Elena: Thanks. What will participants actually do?
Tariq: They’ll introduce themselves to a partner and share one interest.
Elena: That is clear. I can explain those steps to the new members.
notice: Tariq explains the expression without blaming Elena for asking, then gives the practical steps she needs.
response: For a multilingual audience, I would choose clear words and explain unfamiliar expressions. That does not mean removing every interesting phrase. It means noticing when a phrase gets in the way. If I say we will break the ice, I should also explain what participants will do. I can pause after each instruction and invite questions. Instead of only asking whether everyone understands, I can ask a partner to explain the first step in their own words. If the meaning is unclear, I can repair my message. Communication is a shared responsibility, not a test of whose accent sounds most familiar.
frames: Let me put that another way.
By that expression, I mean…
Could you tell me what you’ll do first?
transfer: Explain a welcome activity without relying on unexplained idioms or abbreviations. Ask a partner to tell you the first two steps, then improve your explanation.

listening.title: Making the welcome clear
listening.script: Our international student group was planning a welcome event at the library. The organizer said we would break the ice at ten on Saturday morning. One new member asked whether that meant an outdoor activity. The organizer thanked her for asking and explained that break the ice meant helping people feel comfortable talking. The first activity would be indoors: introduce yourself to a partner and share one interest. A second person asked whether ten meant morning or evening, so the organizer wrote ten in the morning on the agenda. Before moving on, she asked two volunteers to explain the first activity in their own words. Their explanations showed that the instructions were now clear. The group kept the friendly expression, but added plain instructions that everyone could use.

questions.prompt: Where would the welcome event take place?
questions.evidence: a welcome event at the library

questions.prompt: What did one member first think break the ice might mean?
questions.evidence: whether that meant an outdoor activity

questions.prompt: What would partners share after introducing themselves?
questions.evidence: share one interest

questions.prompt: What time and day were confirmed?
questions.evidence: at ten on Saturday morning

questions.prompt: How did the organizer check that the first activity was clear?
questions.answer: By asking two volunteers to explain it in their own words.
questions.evidence: asked two volunteers to explain the first activity in their own words

listening.gist: A group makes an idiom and event instructions clear for a multilingual audience.
